description: A Team, an Expedition and a Resonance. We are a small group of astronomy enthusiasts working towards a greater mission, tackling the challenge of the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser, looking forward to allowing us to visualise and compare landing sites on the Moon seamlessly for future missions. We hope that, with our research, we will be able to change lunar missions for the greater good
summary:
Project Serenity – Lunar Exploration and Mission Planning

Project Serenity is an interactive lunar exploration and mission-planning platform designed to support future lunar missions. It combines three key features into one comprehensive website.

The Lunar Explorer features an interactive 3D map of the Moon, allowing users to select specific dates and identify potentially suitable landing coordinates based on environmental conditions and landing-site suitability.

The Mission Explorer provides a historical overview of previous lunar missions, displaying their journeys and trajectories to the Moon through interactive 3D visualisations, helping users explore the history of lunar exploration.

The Payload Explorer serves as an extensive encyclopedia featuring 320 lunar payloads, providing descriptions, technical information, transportation considerations and details about their intended applications on the lunar surface.

By integrating interactive 3D visualisation, historical mission data and detailed payload information, Project Serenity makes lunar exploration more accessible, informative and engaging while providing valuable insights into the planning, technology and challenges involved in future lunar missions.

1. Project Overview

Serenity is an interactive 3D Lunar Explorer and scientific mission-planning platform developed in response to NASA's CLPS Lunar Mission Browser challenge. Its primary objective is to provide an intuitive yet scientifically grounded environment for exploring the Moon, investigating potential lunar landing sites and understanding how changing astronomical conditions and local terrain influence surface operations, particularly in the lunar south-polar region.

Selecting a suitable lunar landing site involves much more than identifying a relatively flat area on the Moon. Mission planners must consider terrain elevation, crater walls, sunlight availability, visibility of Earth, changing illumination conditions and the timing of operational opportunities. These factors can vary significantly across relatively small distances, especially around the lunar poles, where low solar elevation angles allow crater rims and surrounding terrain to obstruct sunlight for extended periods.

Serenity brings these different considerations together in one interactive platform. Rather than presenting lunar information as disconnected maps, charts or static datasets, it allows users to explore a navigable three-dimensional Moon while simultaneously investigating the scientific conditions associated with selected locations and simulation times.

2. What Does Serenity Do?

The Lunar Explorer provides an integrated environment for visualizing, investigating and comparing lunar locations and their potential suitability for future exploration missions.

Its main capabilities include:

Interactive three-dimensional lunar exploration.

Multiple lunar camera perspectives and an orbital visualization.

Custom lunar location selection and candidate landing-site investigation.

A synchronized simulation clock for exploring different dates and times.

Real-time astronomical positioning of the Sun and Earth relative to selected lunar locations.

Terrain-aware solar illumination and local horizon analysis.

Solar and Earth visibility calculations at different visibility thresholds.

Solar-power estimation and operational-condition analysis.

Regional terrain comparisons and mission-window calculations.

A south-polar visibility atlas with temporal replay.

Permanent Shadowed Region (PSR) reference maps.

Interactive timelines, scenario comparisons and downloadable analytical reports.

These capabilities are designed to help users understand not only what a lunar location looks like, but also how its environment changes and how those changes may influence mission planning.

3. Interactive 3D Lunar Environment

At the centre of Serenity is an interactive three-dimensional representation of the Moon, developed using Three.js.

Users can navigate the lunar globe, rotate it, inspect different geographical regions and examine the lunar surface from multiple perspectives. Dedicated camera views allow exploration of the near side, far side, north pole and south pole. An additional orbital visualization provides a different perspective of the Moon's position and its surrounding astronomical geometry.

The environment uses lunar surface imagery and elevation information to provide geographical context. The near-side and far-side views help users understand the Moon's global geography, while the polar perspectives make it easier to investigate regions that are particularly important for future lunar exploration.

Users can select locations on the lunar surface and use them as the basis for further scientific investigation. The selected location becomes the reference point for the associated local horizon, astronomical visibility and mission-analysis tools.

The purpose of the 3D environment is not simply visual presentation. It acts as the geographical interface connecting the user to the scientific analysis performed throughout Serenity.

4. Simulation Clock and Astronomical Environment

A central feature of Serenity is its shared simulation clock.

Users can change the simulated date and time to investigate how the lunar environment evolves. The astronomical calculations and time-dependent visualizations use this common simulation state, allowing different parts of the platform to remain synchronized.

The platform calculates the positions and directions of the Sun and Earth relative to the Moon and selected surface locations. These calculations make it possible to investigate how celestial bodies appear from the lunar surface and how their positions change throughout a mission timeline.

This is especially important near the lunar poles. Unlike locations near the lunar equator, polar locations can experience extremely low solar elevation angles. Consequently, relatively small changes in the Sun's position can determine whether sunlight reaches a particular location or is obstructed by nearby terrain.

By allowing users to move through simulation time, Serenity transforms astronomical conditions into something that can be explored interactively rather than understood only through static calculations.

5. Lunar Solar Intelligence (LSI)

Lunar Solar Intelligence, or LSI, is one of Serenity's central scientific analysis systems.

LSI investigates sunlight availability and terrain obstruction at selected lunar locations. It combines the Sun's astronomical position with the local surface orientation and surrounding lunar topography to evaluate whether sunlight can reach a particular location.

A particularly important component is the local terrain horizon. The surrounding landscape can obstruct the Sun even when the Sun is geometrically above the general lunar horizon. This is especially significant around polar craters, where elevated crater rims can block low-angle sunlight.

Serenity distinguishes between three different levels of solar visibility:

Sun-centre visibility: Whether the centre of the Sun is above the local terrain skyline.

Any-disk visibility: Whether any portion of the apparent solar disk is visible above the terrain skyline.

Full-disk visibility: Whether the entire apparent solar disk is unobstructed.

These distinctions provide a more informative understanding of illumination than a simple illuminated-or-dark classification.

LSI also presents local horizon information and solar-position data, allowing users to investigate the relationship between the surrounding terrain and the Sun's apparent position.

6. Solar-Power and Surface-Operation Analysis

Serenity includes a solar-power modelling system that provides additional information about potential surface operations.

The model considers factors including solar visibility, the direction of incoming sunlight, the orientation of the selected surface and the selected panel configuration. It estimates potential electrical output under the modelled conditions and allows users to investigate how changing illumination affects estimated power availability.

This adds an operational perspective to the astronomical analysis. Instead of considering sunlight only as a visual phenomenon, users can examine its potential relevance to equipment and surface operations.

The model also demonstrates why solar visibility and solar-power availability should not be treated as identical. A location may have partial solar visibility while its terrain or surface orientation prevents the model from producing useful output.

The resulting estimates are model-based assessments rather than measurements from actual lunar equipment.

7. Earth Visibility and Potential Communication Opportunities

In addition to sunlight, Serenity investigates the visibility of Earth from selected lunar surface locations.

Earth visibility is important because maintaining communication with Earth is a major consideration in lunar mission planning. Local terrain can obstruct the Earth's apparent position, particularly in regions surrounded by high crater walls.

Serenity evaluates Earth visibility using three geometric conditions:

Earth-centre visibility: Whether the centre of Earth's apparent disk is above the local terrain skyline.

Any-disk visibility: Whether at least part of Earth's apparent disk is visible.

Full-disk visibility: Whether the entire apparent disk is unobstructed.

These separate conditions help users understand the difference between a completely obstructed Earth, partial visibility and an unobstructed view.

The platform can display these conditions through local sky visualizations, mission timelines and regional comparisons. This allows users to investigate when Earth may be geometrically visible from a selected site.

Importantly, geometric visibility does not guarantee a functioning communication link. Antenna characteristics, spacecraft orientation, ground-station availability and radio-link budgets would require additional analysis.

8. Local Terrain, Elevation Data and Horizon Analysis

A major scientific challenge in lunar exploration is understanding how local topography affects environmental conditions.

Serenity incorporates lunar elevation information derived from NASA's Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) datasets. These elevation datasets provide the geographical foundation for terrain-related analysis.

The platform uses terrain information to construct local horizon profiles and evaluate whether surrounding topographic features obstruct the apparent directions of the Sun and Earth.

This is particularly relevant in polar regions, where even relatively small changes in terrain elevation can have significant effects on visibility.

Serenity also incorporates regional terrain profiles and comparisons, allowing users to investigate how different locations experience different visibility conditions.

The analytical terrain horizon is distinct from the visual lighting and shading used by the 3D globe. This distinction is important because visually illuminated terrain does not automatically establish that a particular location has an unobstructed astronomical view.

9. South-Polar Visibility Atlas and Shadow Replay

Serenity includes a dedicated south-polar visibility atlas designed to make regional illumination and visibility patterns easier to investigate.

The atlas evaluates 49 selected locations arranged in a south-polar stereographic grid, with approximately 4 km projected spacing. These locations provide a comparative view of how solar and Earth visibility vary across the selected polar region.

Users can investigate different visibility conditions, examine accumulated visibility hours over selected periods and explore the results through temporal replay.

The atlas supports different solar and Earth visibility thresholds, including centre, partial-disk and full-disk conditions. Users can play, pause, step through and scrub the replay while the shared simulation clock updates.

Individual atlas locations can also be selected for further investigation using LSI.

The atlas is particularly useful for demonstrating that two nearby lunar locations can experience substantially different illumination and visibility conditions because of their surrounding terrain.

It is important to distinguish this sampled atlas from a continuous, high-resolution classification of every point across the lunar south pole. Its 49 locations are analytical comparison points rather than a complete surface-wide map.

10. Permanent Shadowed Regions

Serenity also incorporates reference maps of lunar Permanent Shadowed Regions (PSRs).

These regions are particularly significant in lunar exploration because certain polar locations may remain permanently shadowed under long-term astronomical conditions.

The platform includes NASA-derived polar-region reference datasets that allow users to examine the relationship between candidate locations and known shadowed-region classifications.

These reference classifications are different from the time-dependent illumination calculations performed by Serenity. A location experiencing temporary darkness at a particular simulation time is not necessarily permanently shadowed.

Combining these two types of information helps users distinguish between long-term polar environmental characteristics and changing local illumination conditions.

11. Mission Window Finder and Site Comparison

Serenity includes mission-window analysis tools that help users investigate when selected environmental conditions are satisfied.

The Mission Window Finder evaluates time-dependent visibility conditions and identifies intervals during which specified criteria are met.

Users can examine solar and Earth visibility windows, investigate qualifying periods and compare candidate locations under different mission requirements.

The system distinguishes between different visibility thresholds and can combine conditions to investigate periods when multiple requirements are satisfied simultaneously.

Regional comparisons provide another way to evaluate candidate locations. Users can compare sites, examine differences in their terrain-dependent visibility and investigate how changing simulation dates affects their potential operational opportunities.

Additional comparison and ranking capabilities allow scenarios to be evaluated using criteria such as qualifying time, Earth-centre blackout duration and modelled energy.

Analytical results can also be exported as JSON reports, allowing scenario information and calculated results to be retained for further examination.

12. Technologies and Development Tools

Serenity was developed as a browser-based application using a combination of modern web technologies and scientific datasets.

Programming languages:

TypeScript — application logic, scientific calculations, data structures and component integration.

JavaScript — supporting application functionality.

CSS — interface styling, layouts and visual presentation.

Development frameworks and libraries:

React — interactive user interface and application components.

Three.js — three-dimensional lunar environment, camera navigation and orbital visualization.

Vite — development server and production build system.

Astronomy Engine — astronomical calculations and simulation support.

Scientific datasets and references:

NASA LOLA lunar elevation datasets — lunar surface topography and terrain analysis.

NASA lunar imagery and polar-region datasets — geographical visualization and reference mapping.

JPL DE421 ephemeris data — astronomical positioning and celestial calculations.

Hardware and deployment:

Serenity is designed to operate on ordinary computers with a compatible modern web browser and WebGL2 support. It does not require specialized lunar hardware or dedicated scientific workstations. The application can be distributed as a browser-based website, making its interactive environment accessible without requiring users to install a separate desktop application.

13. What Makes Serenity Creative and Innovative?

The main innovation behind Serenity is its integration of several different areas of lunar science into one interactive environment.

Traditional lunar maps can show geographical information, while astronomical calculations can describe celestial positions and scientific reports can present mission-analysis results. However, understanding how these factors interact at a particular lunar location and time can be challenging.

Serenity connects these elements.

A user can explore the Moon in three dimensions, select a location, adjust the simulation clock, investigate its local terrain horizon, examine solar and Earth visibility, explore polar conditions and compare potential mission windows without leaving the same application.

Another important aspect is its distinction between visual appearance and analytical results. The platform does not rely solely on the apparent lighting of the 3D Moon to determine whether a location is illuminated. It incorporates separate terrain-aware calculations to investigate the actual geometrical relationship between the local landscape and celestial bodies.

Its combination of global exploration, local terrain analysis, polar visibility comparisons and time-dependent mission planning makes Serenity more than a conventional lunar visualization tool.

14. Factors Considered During Development

Throughout development, our team considered several important factors:

Scientific accuracy: Astronomical positions, lunar orientation and terrain-dependent visibility needed to be based on appropriate scientific data and calculations.

Terrain representation: Lunar topography is especially important near the poles, where crater rims and elevation differences can obstruct sunlight and Earth visibility.

Time dependence: Environmental conditions change throughout a mission, so a shared simulation clock and temporal analysis were essential.

Usability: Scientific information needed to be presented through understandable visualizations, interactive controls and comparisons.

Performance: Three-dimensional rendering and terrain analysis needed to operate efficiently in a web browser.

Accessibility: The platform needed to be usable on standard computers without specialized equipment.

Scientific limitations: We considered the distinction between geometric visibility, modelled solar power, permanent shadow classifications and actual communication availability.

15. Intended Impact

Our intended impact is to make lunar mission-planning information more accessible, understandable and useful for evaluating potential exploration locations.

As lunar exploration expands, particularly through robotic missions and future human exploration, understanding the relationship between local terrain, sunlight and Earth visibility becomes increasingly important.

Serenity aims to help students, researchers, educators and mission-planning enthusiasts investigate these conditions through an interactive scientific environment.

By bringing three-dimensional lunar exploration together with astronomical calculations, terrain-aware analysis, polar visibility mapping and mission-window comparisons, Serenity provides a unified way to explore the challenges of operating on the lunar surface.

Ultimately, our vision is to transform lunar exploration from simply viewing the Moon into actively investigating its environment, comparing potential landing sites and understanding the scientific conditions that could shape future missions.
